content: The testing process evaluates the differences in the prevalence of HIV drug resistance between populations exposed to antiretroviral (ARV) drugs for the prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) and those with unknown exposure. This is done to guide the selection of the most effective first-line antiretroviral therapy (ART) for these populations. National strategies for assessing HIV drug resistance should be developed and routinely implemented as part of comprehensive HIV treatment programs. The recommendations outlined in these guidelines may necessitate modifications to existing monitoring and evaluation systems. Guidance is available on the 12 components of a monitoring and evaluation system, along with tools to review and strengthen national HIV monitoring and evaluation frameworks. Specific areas for review are highlighted to ensure alignment with the updated ARV guidelines. The World Health Organization (WHO) clinical staging of HIV disease in adults, adolescents, and children is detailed in Annex 1. This staging system is adapted from WHO case definitions for HIV surveillance and revised clinical staging and immunological classification of HIV-related disease. For example, clinical stage 3 includes symptomatic lymphoid interstitial pneumonitis and chronic HIV-associated lung disease, while stage 4 includes conditions such as HIV wasting syndrome, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, recurrent severe bacterial pneumonia, chronic herpes simplex infection, esophageal candidiasis, extrapulmonary tuberculosis, Kaposi sarcoma, and central nervous system toxoplasmosis, among others. The 2013 recommendations for ART initiation in adults and adolescents prioritize treatment for individuals with severe or advanced symptomatic disease (WHO clinical stage 3 or 4) or those with a CD4 count ≤ 350 cells/mm³, regardless of clinical symptoms. Active tuberculosis (TB) disease refers to the period when TB progresses from latency to active disease, while latent TB infection indicates successful immune containment of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. For pregnant and breastfeeding women with HIV, lifelong ART is recommended (Option B+), with the preferred regimen being tenofovir (TDF) + lamivudine (3TC) or emtricitabine (FTC) + efavirenz (EFV). Early infant diagnosis is critical, with testing recommended at birth or the first postnatal visit (4–6 weeks). ART should be initiated immediately if indicated, with confirmatory testing conducted simultaneously. For children under five years of age, ART initiation is recommended for those with WHO clinical stage 3 or 4 disease or a CD4 count ≤ 750 cells/mm³ or < 25%, whichever is lower. For children older than five years, ART should be initiated at WHO clinical stage 3 or 4 or with a CD4 count ≤ 350 cells/mm³. Stavudine (d4T) use should be restricted to cases where toxicity to zidovudine (AZT) is suspected or confirmed, and alternatives such as abacavir (ABC) or TDF are unavailable. The readiness assessment checklist for transitioning to ART for pregnant and breastfeeding women addresses issues ranging from national policy to facility readiness. It includes considerations for political commitment, financial planning, service delivery models, human resource capacity, ARV regimen choice, supply chain management, and monitoring and evaluation systems. For example, the checklist emphasizes the need for national endorsement of task-shifting strategies, training of healthcare workers, and the establishment of pharmacovigilance systems. Monitoring and evaluation systems should allow for documentation of ART initiation versus continuation during antenatal care and PMTCT services. This ensures comprehensive tracking of treatment outcomes and program effectiveness.
